promo-sub-white.title: In sublimation, white is not a colour #shorts
promo-sub-white.description:
There is no white ink in sublimation. Every white area in your design is not printed at all — it is a window onto whatever the blank is.

Press this design on a white mug and it is exactly what you drew, because every white area is left alone and what shows through is a white mug.

Same file, same press, on a pale blue mug. The lettering inside the banner is blue. The starburst has gone see-through — the navy outline is still there, but the middle of it is mug.

Nothing failed. The file was always like this and the white mug was hiding it.

The fix takes ten seconds: drop a mid-tone rectangle behind your whole design in Canva and look at what survives. Anything that changes colour was never ink.

promo-sub-polyester.title: Sublimation does not work on cotton #shorts
promo-sub-polyester.description:
Epson, who make the printers, put the rule in one line: dye-sublimation printing requires polyester fabrics or polymer-coated surfaces.

That is not a preference. The dye turns to gas and bonds with polyester. On cotton there is nothing for it to bond to, so it sits on the surface looking completely acceptable — for about one wash. Then it is gone.

Hard goods are the same rule in a different form. Mugs, tumblers, slate, metal signs: they are not polyester, they are coated with a polymer, and that coating is what takes the dye. An uncoated mug from a supermarket will take nothing at all.

And light blanks only. On a dark blank the ink is translucent and simply disappears into it.

promo-sub-myth.title: The transparent PNG rule everyone gets backwards #shorts
promo-sub-myth.description:
Everyone tells you to export a transparent PNG or you will get a white box. That is true for print on demand, where a provider lays white ink onto a dark shirt. It is not true for sublimation.

Your sublimation printer has no white ink at all, so a white background and a transparent background do exactly the same thing. No ink. The blank shows through.

Which sounds like good news and is the opposite. It means a white rectangle you forgot about costs you nothing, and a white starburst you were relying on costs you everything — and the file looks identical either way.

So export transparent anyway. Not for the printer. For you. On a transparent PNG you can see the windows: open it on a dark background and every window lights up.

promo-sub-mirror.title: Mirrored twice is the same as not mirrored #shorts
promo-sub-mirror.description:
Sublimation prints onto paper and then you press the paper face down onto the blank, so the image flips. Something in the chain has to mirror it.

Canva has a flip — select everything, Flip, Horizontal.

But most sublimation printer software mirrors for you automatically, and some of it does so without telling you. Mirror in Canva as well and you have mirrored twice, which is the same as not mirroring at all — and you find out when the text comes out backwards on a blank you have just paid for.

So check your printer software first. If it mirrors, do nothing in Canva. If it does not, flip in Canva. One or the other, never both — and write down which one you chose.
